scope: Österreich · Zivil- und Strafverfahren (getrennt gekennzeichnete Verweise)

esig_regulation.basis: Regulation (EU) No 910/2014 as amended by Regulation (EU) 2024/1183; Signatur- und Vertrauensdienstegesetz (SVG), BGBl. I Nr. 50/2016. SVG § 4(1): a qualified electronic signature meets the written-form requirement of § 886 ABGB; other statutory or agreed form requirements remain.

data_access_basis.basis: A private party needs a lawful basis under GDPR Art. 6(1), for example legitimate interests (Art. 6(1)(f)); data on criminal offences needs official authority or a legal authorisation (Art. 10). A person can request their own data (Art. 15) within the Art. 12(3) period. Processing for the investigation and prosecution of criminal offences is governed by DSG Part 3 (§§ 36 ff.).

timestamp_recognition.basis: Art. 41(1): a time stamp is not denied legal effect or admissibility solely because it is electronic or not qualified. Art. 41(2): a qualified time stamp is presumed accurate as to date and time and integrity of the bound data. Art. 42(1) sets the qualified requirements; Art. 24a(6) recognises qualified time stamps across Member States. No separate Austrian time-stamp rule was identified in SVG § 4.

evidence_rules.basis: The court decides by free conviction, after careful consideration of the whole hearing and taking of evidence, whether a factual statement is true, unless the law provides otherwise.

Public and private documents may be created on paper or electronically. A signed private document gives full proof that its statements come from the signatory; this does not attach to a software export as such.
The judgment may rely only on what was presented at the main hearing; file documents serve as evidence only if read out or summarised there.
Experts are appointed where investigations or the taking of evidence need special expertise that the prosecuting authorities do not have.
